title: Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates
part: IV: Orbits, stars, and black holes
one_line_summary: Finishes the coordinate-singularity programme begun with Rindler and Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates: exponentiating the Schwarzschild null coordinates yields the Kruskal metric, whose 45-degree light cones make horizons, infall, signal delays, the four-region maximal extension (wormhole, white hole), and the Kruskal Penrose diagram with its trapped surfaces all readable by eye, with the Minkowski-versus-accelerating-frame analogy explaining why the construction is natural.
role_in_book: Third of the black-hole geometry chapters in Part IV. Chapter 25 introduced the tortoise coordinate and the infalling astronaut, Chapter 26 set up the problem (closed trapped surfaces, the Rindler toy model tamed by exponentiated null coordinates, and Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates that only half-fix r = 2M). This chapter applies the Rindler recipe to Schwarzschild to get one global chart, then uses it to settle causal questions (what can escape, what can be seen, whether the extension is traversable) and to redraw the black hole on a Penrose diagram, reusing the conformal toolkit of Chapter 19. It closes the geometric treatment of Schwarzschild and sets up Chapter 28, where the Rindler picture of the near-horizon region and exponential redshift feed the Unruh and Hawking radiation arguments.

assumed_background.topic: Schwarzschild metric, event horizon at r = 2M and the difference between coordinate and physical singularities
Tortoise coordinate r* and its logarithmic behaviour near r = 2M
Eddington-Finkelstein null coordinates U = t - r*, V = t + r* and the metric -(1 - 2M/r) dU dV
Rindler spacetime and removal of its x = 0 coordinate singularity by exponentiating null coordinates
Closed trapped surfaces as a signal of a singularity
Uniformly accelerated world line as a hyperbola X^2 - T^2 = g^-2
Penrose diagrams, conformal infinities i+, i-, i0, scri+/-, singularities as boundaries
Radial infall of an astronaut, redshift and slowing of signals seen from outside
Minkowski spacetime diagrams, light cones, light-cone coordinates
Hyperbolic functions sinh, cosh, tanh, artanh and their identities

assumed_background.where: GA Appendix D (Embedding); not developed in the main text before this chapter

assumed_background.topic: Connection coefficients and covariant acceleration (for Exercise 27.4)

learning_objectives: Reader can carry out the chain Schwarzschild -> tortoise/null coordinates (U, V) -> exponentiated null coordinates (u, v) -> Kruskal (T, X) and obtain the Kruskal line element.
Reader can explain why the Kruskal metric is regular at r = 2M and why this proves the Schwarzschild radius is only a coordinate singularity.
Reader can use the implicit relations (1 - r/2M) e^{r/2M} = T^2 - X^2 and T/X = tanh(t/4M) to locate constant-r hyperbolae, constant-t rays, the horizons X = +/-T and the singularities T^2 - X^2 = 1.
Reader can identify regions I, II, I', II' of the Kruskal diagram and say which part the original Schwarzschild chart (outside and inside) covers.

Reader can draw an infalling timelike world line and a hovering observer's hyperbola, and explain from 45-degree light rays why received pulses thin out and why pulses from inside the horizon never arrive.
Reader can state the Rindler analogy: Kruskal coordinates are to Schwarzschild coordinates as inertial Minkowski coordinates are to accelerating (Rindler) coordinates.
Reader can derive the Rindler metric from the hyperbolic transformation T = x sinh t, X = x cosh t and read x as the inverse proper acceleration.
Reader can describe the maximal Kruskal extension as two asymptotically flat exteriors joined by a (non-traversable) Einstein-Rosen bridge, with a black-hole region II and a white-hole region II'.
Reader can argue, both from the Kruskal diagram and from a sequence of spacelike slices, that no causal signal can pass from region I to region I'.
Reader can explain why the Schwarzschild geometry is static only in regions I and I' and why slices through II and II' evolve (pinch-off of the throat).
Reader can sketch and label the Penrose diagram of the Kruskal extension (i+, i-, i0, scri+/-, horizons, spacelike singularities) and contrast it with Robertson-Walker diagrams.
Reader can use constant-r and constant-t lines on the Penrose diagram to show that light fronts emitted inside the horizon have shrinking area (trapped surfaces).
Reader can show that a uniformly accelerating observer sees a plane wave exponentially redshifted as Omega e^{-g tau}, linking horizon redshift to acceleration.

teaching_approach.summary: A short, picture-centred chapter. The algebra is dispatched quickly by explicitly re-running the recipe the reader already used on Rindler space in Chapter 26, so the new content is almost entirely interpretive: a sequence of Kruskal diagrams (full grid, constant r, constant t, infall, signals) trains the eye to read causal structure off 45-degree light rays. When the coordinates still feel artificial, the authors invert the reader's intuition with Rindler's analogy, making Kruskal the 'natural' inertial-like chart and Schwarzschild the awkward accelerated one. The extension to the whole plane is then interpreted physically (second universe, wormhole, white hole) and immediately tamed by causal arguments and a flip-book of embedding diagrams showing the throat pinching off. The chapter ends by recycling the Penrose-diagram toolkit of Chapter 19 and closing the loop to the trapped-surface motivation of Chapter 26. Exercises push the Rindler connection toward exponential redshift, preparing Hawking radiation.
narrative_arc: Recall the unfinished business: Eddington-Finkelstein charts each fix only one family of radial light rays at r = 2M; the metric was left as a function times dU dV.
Example 27.1: use r* = (V - U)/2 to factor the prefactor into a regular function of r, an exponential in V - U, and the flat light-cone form.
Copy the Rindler move: exponentiate the null coordinates to absorb the exponential, then form timelike and spacelike combinations T and X to get the Kruskal metric.
Check: the conformal factor 32M^3 e^{-r/2M}/r is finite at r = 2M, so the Schwarzschild radius is a coordinate artefact; all radial light rays are at 45 degrees.
Tour the Kruskal diagram: constant-r hyperbolae, horizons as X = +/-T, two r = 0 singularity hyperbolae, straight constant-t lines, and which quadrants Schwarzschild coordinates cover.
Application (Example 27.2): infalling astronaut and a hovering observer exchanging light pulses, read directly off the diagram.
Raise the puzzle of the uncovered half-plane (regions I' and II') and name the Kruskal extension.
Build intuition (Example 27.3): hyperbolic coordinates in flat space give the Rindler metric, whose structure mirrors Schwarzschild; state the Minkowski:accelerating = Kruskal:Schwarzschild analogy.
Interpret the extension: region I' as a second asymptotically flat universe, region II' as a white hole, the T = 0 slice as a wormhole throat of radius 2M.
Test traversability: no causal curve joins I and I'; Example 27.4 re-tells this dynamically as a sequence of slices where the throat opens and pinches off too quickly.

Compactify: the Penrose diagram of the extension, with spacelike singularities on its edges, asymptotic infinities, and a comment that the visible past singularity is an artefact of the idealized extension.
Close the loop (Example 27.5): read constant-r lines on the Penrose diagram to show outgoing and ingoing fronts both shrink inside the horizon, justifying the trapped surfaces of Chapter 26.
Exercises: verify the metric and coordinate relations, Rindler observers and their acceleration, and exponential redshift for uniform acceleration.
signature_moves: Explicitly reuse the Rindler three-step recipe (null coordinates, exponentiate, rotate to T and X) so the Schwarzschild computation feels like a repeat, not a trick.
Factorize a singular-looking metric into (regular function) x (exponential of null coordinates) x (flat light-cone metric) to show exactly which piece the coordinate change must absorb.
Replace algebraic causal arguments with visual ones: once every radial light ray is at 45 degrees, questions like 'can a signal reach region I prime?' are answered by looking.
Analogy table (eqn 27.12) reversing the reader's sense of which coordinates are natural: Kruskal behaves like inertial coordinates, Schwarzschild like a rocket's accelerating frame.
Flip-book of embedding diagrams paired with horizontal slices on the Kruskal diagram to animate a wormhole opening and pinching shut.
Reading a Penrose diagram with a coordinate grid by 'moving up to the next side-to-side line' to decide whether wavefront areas grow or shrink.
Exercises that tie a geometric feature (horizon) to a kinematic effect (exponential redshift of an accelerated observer), seeding the next chapter.

sections.title: Chapter opening
sections.summary: After a Thomas Hardy epigraph on the mortality of stars, the authors state the goal inherited from Chapter 26: a single chart that is continuous across the horizon and still intuitive. Margin notes give short biographies of Martin Kruskal and George Szekeres.
key_moves: Frame the chapter as the answer to the open problem of Chapter 26

sections.title: Enter the Kruskal metric
sections.summary: Explains why Eddington-Finkelstein charts are unsatisfactory (each smooths only ingoing or only outgoing rays at r_S), restarts from ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r) dU dV, rewrites the prefactor via the tortoise relation, exponentiates the null coordinates exactly as for Rindler space, and forms T and X to obtain the Kruskal metric (27.6), regular at r = 2M. The inverse relations are given in a margin note.
key_moves: Substitute r* = (V - U)/2 to write 1 - 2M/r = (2M/r) e^{-r/2M} e^{(V-U)/4M}.
Define u = -e^{-U/4M}, v = e^{V/4M}, so du dv carries the factor e^{(V-U)/4M}/16M^2 that cancels the exponential.
Result ds^2 = -(32M^3 e^{-r/2M}/r) du dv, then T = (u + v)/2, X = (v - u)/2 gives a conformal factor times -dT^2 + dX^2.
Observe the prefactor is finite and non-zero at r = 2M: the horizon singularity is gone.

sections.title: Reading the Kruskal diagram and the infalling astronaut
sections.summary: A guided tour of the X-T plane: constant-r curves are hyperbolae, r = 2M becomes the crossed lines X = +/-T dividing the plane into four regions, r = 0 is a pair of spacelike hyperbolae T^2 - X^2 = 1 (past and future), constant-t surfaces are straight lines through the origin, and Schwarzschild coordinates cover only the half-plane T > -X (region I outside, region II inside). Example 27.2 then shows an astronaut crossing into region II and a hovering observer on a hyperbola receiving ever sparser pulses, while pulses sent from inside end on the singularity.
concepts: Kruskal regions I, II, I', II'
key_moves: Each point of the diagram stands for a 2-sphere of area 4 pi r^2.
r = 2M gives X^2 - T^2 = 0, so the horizon is a pair of null lines.
t is a hyperbolic angle: t = +infinity on X = T, t = -infinity on X = -T, and t = 0 on T = 0 outside but on X = 0 inside.
Causal questions reduce to checking whether a path can stay within 45 degrees of vertical.

sections.title: Rindler analogy (Example 27.3)
sections.summary: Motivates the still-strange coordinates using Wolfgang Rindler's analogy. Hyperbolic coordinates T = x sinh t, X = x cosh t in flat space describe a family of uniformly accelerated observers with proper acceleration 1/x, and the Minkowski metric becomes the Rindler metric; swapping sinh and cosh covers the future and past wedges. A further substitution produces a line element shaped like Schwarzschild, giving the correspondence Minkowski:Kruskal as accelerating:Schwarzschild. Margin notes discuss rigid acceleration (the back of a rocket must accelerate harder) and why constant-t lines are straight.
key_moves: Recall that X^2 - T^2 = x^2 is the world line of constant proper acceleration 1/x.
Apply the hyperbolic change of variables and compute -dT^2 + dX^2 = -x^2 dt^2 + dx^2 in the right wedge.
Use T = x cosh t, X = x sinh t in the top and bottom wedges, where the roles of the time and space coordinates are exchanged.
Substitute x^2 = 2r - 1 (with a sign flip inside) to make one formula resemble the Schwarzschild metric in all wedges.
Conclude that the Kruskal chart is the 'inertial' one and the Schwarzschild chart the accelerated one.

sections.title: Wormholes
sections.summary: Takes the whole Kruskal plane seriously. Region I' is asymptotically flat at large negative X, so it is another exterior universe; region II' is reached only by past-directed curves from I', making its past singularity a white hole, and the primed side runs with t reversed. The T = 0 slice is an embedding-diagram wormhole with a throat of radius 2M joining the two universes. Nevertheless no timelike or null curve joins I and I'. Example 27.4 shows the spacelike slices are not static beyond the horizons: moving the slice up in T, the two sheets are separate, meet at a pinch, open into a throat of maximum radius 2M at T = 0, and pinch off again before any signal could cross.
concepts: time reversal of the primed universe
dynamical evolution of the wormhole throat
key_moves: Asymptotic flatness at X -> -infinity identifies region I' as a second exterior.
Past-directed world lines fall from I' into II' just as future-directed ones fall from I into II, so II' is a time-reversed black hole.
Light cones at 45 degrees show no causal curve from I to I'.
Stack embedding diagrams for horizontal slices at increasing T to show the throat opening and closing faster than light could cross.

sections.title: Another Penrose diagram
sections.summary: Presents the conformal diagram of the Kruskal extension: the two exteriors, the black- and white-hole regions, horizontal spacelike singularities at the top and bottom edges, and the infinities i+, i-, i0 and scri+/- that exist because each exterior is asymptotically flat. Unlike Robertson-Walker models, not every world line ends on a singularity. The past singularity is visible from region I (called naked here) and is blamed on the idealized extension. A grid of constant-r and constant-t lines is added, and Example 27.5 uses it to show that inside the horizon both outgoing and ingoing light fronts move to smaller r, i.e. trapped surfaces.
concepts: spacelike singularity as boundary of spacetime
Kruskal regions I, II, I', II'
key_moves: Compactify so that singularities and infinities sit at the finite edges of the diagram.
Contrast with Robertson-Walker Penrose diagrams where all world lines meet the singularity.
Rotate the role of the grid lines: inside the horizon, 'side to side' lines are constant r, so the next future moment has smaller r.
Outgoing and ingoing fronts both shrink in region II: closed trapped surfaces, confirming the Chapter 26 motivation.

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises
sections.summary: The summary lists three points: Kruskal coordinates remove the r_S singularity and invite an extension, their relation to Schwarzschild parallels inertial versus accelerating Minkowski coordinates, and the conformal picture places the singularity at the edge of spacetime. Five exercises verify the coordinate algebra, treat Rindler observers and their covariant acceleration, and derive exponential redshift for a uniformly accelerating observer.
key_moves: Exercises connect the Rindler picture to exponential redshift, preparing Hawking and Unruh radiation in Chapter 28.

concepts.name: Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates (T, X, theta, phi) on the Schwarzschild geometry defined implicitly by (1 - r/2M) e^{r/2M} = T^2 - X^2 and T/X = tanh(t/4M) in the exterior, in which the radial part of the metric is a positive function of r times the flat form -dT^2 + dX^2; they are regular across r = 2M and extend to cover the entire maximally extended spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the completion of the Chapter 26 programme: take Eddington-Finkelstein null coordinates, exponentiate them as in the Rindler toy model, then form sum and difference. Interpreted afterwards through a Kruskal diagram and Rindler's analogy.
concepts.notes: The book's T and X are dimensionless (r = 0 sits at T^2 - X^2 = 1). Other texts normalize differently or use the null pair (u, v) directly as 'Kruskal coordinates'.

concepts.name: Kruskal-Szekeres line element
concepts.definition: The Schwarzschild metric written in Kruskal coordinates, ds^2 = (32M^3/r) e^{-r/2M} (-dT^2 + dX^2) + r^2 dOmega^2, with r = r(T, X) given implicitly; its coefficients are finite and non-degenerate at r = 2M and blow up only at r = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained in Example 27.1 and the following text by successive substitutions starting from -(1 - 2M/r) dU dV; checked by noting that nothing goes wrong at r = 2M.
concepts.notes: Asymptotically the conformal factor does not approach 1 in these coordinates; the book's remark that the metric becomes flat as X -> infinity refers to the geometry, not to the component form.

concepts.name: coordinate singularity
concepts.definition: A place where metric components in a particular chart diverge or become degenerate although curvature invariants stay finite, so that a different choice of coordinates removes the problem; r = 2M in Schwarzschild coordinates is the standard example.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited: the Kruskal metric is regular at r = 2M, which the authors present as the definitive demonstration of the claim made in Chapters 25 and 26. A margin note quotes Synge's remark that the singularity would never have been suspected had these coordinates been used first.

concepts.name: curvature singularity at r = 0
concepts.definition: The genuine singularity of the Schwarzschild geometry, where tidal curvature diverges; in Kruskal coordinates it is the pair of spacelike hyperbolae T^2 - X^2 = 1, one to the future (bounding region II) and one to the past (bounding region II').
concepts.how_introduced: Shown as thick lines with the excluded region shaded in every Kruskal diagram; discussed as an 'edge' of spacetime when the Penrose diagram is drawn.
concepts.notes: Because it is spacelike, the future singularity is a moment in the infaller's future, not a point at the centre of space; the book implies this through the diagrams without saying so directly.

concepts.name: tortoise coordinate
concepts.definition: The radial coordinate r* = r + 2M ln|r/2M - 1| for which radial null geodesics of Schwarzschild satisfy t = +/- r* + const; it tends to minus infinity at the horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Used, not re-derived: its expression in terms of the null coordinates, r* = (V - U)/2, is the key substitution of Example 27.1.

concepts.name: Eddington-Finkelstein null coordinates
concepts.definition: Null coordinates U = t - r* (constant along outgoing radial light rays) and V = t + r* (constant along ingoing ones), in which the radial Schwarzschild metric takes the form -(1 - 2M/r) dU dV.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken over from Chapter 26 as the starting point; the chapter opens by pointing out that charts using only one of them leave the other family of rays badly behaved at r_S.
concepts.notes: Capital U, V here are the logarithmic null coordinates, while in the Rindler Example 26.3 capital letters denoted the exponentiated ones: the letter roles are swapped between chapters.

concepts.name: null (light-cone) coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates labelled by families of null curves (in 2D, u = t - x and v = t + x), in which a flat metric reads -du dv; they turn radial light rays into coordinate lines and make light-cone structure explicit.
concepts.how_introduced: Assumed from Chapters 19 and 26 and used as the scaffolding of the construction.

concepts.name: exponential rescaling of null coordinates
concepts.definition: Replacing null coordinates by monotonic exponentials of themselves, e.g. u = -e^{-U/4M}, v = e^{V/4M}, so that a metric of the form (regular function) x e^{(V-U)/4M} dU dV becomes (regular function) x du dv, and the finite ranges of u and v can then be extended past the old coordinate boundary.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the same step already used for Rindler space; its necessity is made visible by first factorizing the metric into a regular r-dependent piece, an exponential of null coordinates, and the flat light-cone metric.
concepts.notes: The rate 1/4M is fixed by the requirement that the exponential cancels exactly; it equals the surface gravity of the hole (not named in this chapter).

concepts.name: conformally flat radial sector
concepts.definition: In Kruskal coordinates the (T, X) part of the metric is a positive function times -dT^2 + dX^2, so radial null rays satisfy dT = +/- dX everywhere and all light cones in the diagram have Minkowski shape.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated right after the metric: by construction every radial null geodesic is a 45-degree line, not just one family as with Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates; future cones point to increasing T.

concepts.name: Kruskal diagram
concepts.definition: A spacetime diagram of the Schwarzschild geometry in the (X, T) plane with angles suppressed, so each point is a 2-sphere; light rays are at 45 degrees, horizons are the diagonals, the r = 0 singularities are hyperbolae, and constant-r and constant-t curves form a hyperbolic grid.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced through Figs 27.1-27.3 and then used as a working tool for infall, signalling, the extension and traversability.

concepts.name: Kruskal regions I, II, I', II'
aliases: four quadrants of the Kruskal diagram
concepts.definition: The four regions into which the horizons X = +/-T divide the Kruskal plane: I (X > |T|) is our exterior, II (T > |X|) the black-hole interior ending at the future singularity, I' (X < -|T|) a second exterior, and II' (T < -|X|) the white-hole interior beginning at the past singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Labelled on Fig. 27.1; the text notes that ordinary Schwarzschild coordinates cover I (r > 2M) and II (r < 2M), i.e. the half-plane T > -X, and that a collapsing star only passes through I and II.

concepts.name: constant-r hyperbolae
concepts.definition: Curves of fixed Schwarzschild radius in the Kruskal plane, X^2 - T^2 = (r/2M - 1) e^{r/2M}: timelike hyperbolae opening left and right for r > 2M, the null diagonals for r = 2M, and spacelike hyperbolae opening up and down for r < 2M, reaching T^2 - X^2 = 1 at r = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Fig. 27.2 plots examples; the first bullet of the diagram tour reads off the horizon and singularity as special members.

concepts.name: constant-t lines in Kruskal coordinates
concepts.definition: Surfaces of fixed Schwarzschild time map to straight lines through the origin of the Kruskal plane: T/X = tanh(t/4M) outside the horizon and X/T = tanh(t/4M) inside, with t -> +infinity on X = T and t -> -infinity on X = -T; t behaves like a boost angle.
concepts.how_introduced: Fig. 27.3 and the third bullet of the diagram tour; margin note 7 gives the analogous statement in Rindler coordinates.
concepts.notes: Inside the horizon constant-t lines are timelike and t is a spatial coordinate; the whole horizon line X = T corresponds to the single value t = +infinity, which is why Schwarzschild time cannot label events on it.

concepts.name: event horizon
concepts.definition: The null surface r = 2M separating events that can send signals to the distant exterior from those that cannot; in Kruskal coordinates it is the pair of 45-degree lines X = +/-T, the future horizon (X = T, T > 0) bounding the black hole and the past horizon (X = -T, T < 0 on the region I side) bounding the white hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as the r = 2M hyperbola that degenerates into straight lines X = +/-T cutting the plane into four regions.

concepts.name: static (hovering) observer
concepts.definition: An observer who keeps a fixed radius r > 2M, which requires continuous thrust; in the Kruskal diagram the world line is a constant-r hyperbola in region I, directly analogous to a uniformly accelerating rocket in Minkowski space.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 27.2 places such an observer on a hyperbola receiving pulses; Example 27.3 explains why this is the natural analogue of a Rindler observer.

concepts.name: infalling observer and signal delay
aliases: infinite delay of signals near the horizon
concepts.definition: A radially infalling body crosses r = 2M at finite proper time; pulses it emits at regular intervals reach a hovering observer at ever longer coordinate-time intervals, the arrival time diverging for emission approaching the horizon, while pulses emitted inside travel at 45 degrees into the future singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 27.2 with Figs 27.4 and 27.5: the result that previously needed integrals is read off a single diagram.
concepts.notes: Links back to the exponential redshift derived in Chapter 26 (time constant 4M).

concepts.name: Rindler coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates (t, x, y, z) on flat spacetime defined in the right wedge by T = x sinh t, X = x cosh t, in which the metric reads -x^2 dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2; curves of constant x are uniformly accelerated world lines with proper acceleration 1/x and lines of constant t are straight rays through the origin. In the top and bottom wedges T = x cosh t, X = x sinh t gives x^2 dt^2 - dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 27.3, credited to Wolfgang Rindler, as a flat-space model whose coordinate behaviour mimics Schwarzschild; builds on the Rindler toy model of Chapter 26.
concepts.notes: The time coordinate t here is a dimensionless boost parameter, unrelated to Schwarzschild t except through the analogy (t_Schwarzschild/4M plays its role).

concepts.name: uniformly accelerated observer
concepts.definition: A world line in flat spacetime with constant proper acceleration g, X^2 - T^2 = g^{-2}, parametrized by proper time as T = g^{-1} sinh(g tau), X = g^{-1} cosh(g tau); it asymptotes to the null lines X = +/-T, which act as horizons for that observer.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 2 in Example 27.3 and used in Exercises 27.3 and 27.5.

concepts.name: Born-rigid acceleration
aliases: differential acceleration of a rigid body
concepts.definition: For an extended body to accelerate without its proper length changing, each point must follow its own hyperbola X^2 - T^2 = x^2 with proper acceleration 1/x, so the rear (smaller x) accelerates harder than the front; seen in the inertial frame the body length-contracts progressively.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 6 and the horizontal bars in Fig. 27.6(a) joining different hyperbolae at equal T.

concepts.name: Rindler-Kruskal analogy
concepts.definition: The correspondence in which inertial Minkowski coordinates play the role of Kruskal coordinates and accelerating (Rindler) coordinates play the role of Schwarzschild coordinates: in both pairs the second chart covers only a wedge, has a coordinate singularity on the null boundary, and its time coordinate is a hyperbolic angle; a hovering Schwarzschild observer corresponds to a rocket.
concepts.how_introduced: Built in Example 27.3 by transforming Minkowski space into hyperbolic coordinates, rewriting the result in a Schwarzschild-like form, and summarized as the analogy (27.12); used to argue Kruskal coordinates are the natural ones.
concepts.notes: Precisely, the near-horizon region of Schwarzschild is Rindler space with proper distance rho = sqrt(8M(r - 2M)) and Rindler time t/4M; the book's global substitution x^2 = 2r - 1 is only a loose resemblance.

concepts.name: Kruskal extension
concepts.definition: The spacetime obtained by letting Kruskal coordinates range over the whole region T^2 - X^2 < 1, adding to the Schwarzschild exterior and interior (I, II) a second exterior I' and a white-hole interior II'; it is the vacuum solution with no star, in which every geodesic either reaches infinity or a singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as a puzzle after Example 27.2 (half the plane is unused), then interpreted physically in Section 27.2 and drawn as a Penrose diagram in Section 27.3; Fig. 27.1's caption stresses that a real collapsing star only uses regions I and II.
prerequisites: Kruskal regions I, II, I', II'
concepts.notes: The authors call the visible past singularity a likely artefact of this artificial extension.

concepts.name: Einstein-Rosen bridge
concepts.definition: The geometry of a spacelike slice of the Kruskal extension through both exteriors: two asymptotically flat sheets joined by a neck whose minimum areal radius is 2M on the T = 0 slice.
concepts.how_introduced: Section 27.2 and Fig. 27.7 via an embedding diagram of the T = 0 slice.
concepts.notes: The book does not use the name Einstein-Rosen bridge; it calls it a wormhole with a throat.

concepts.name: white hole
concepts.definition: The region II' of the Kruskal extension: bounded to the past by the r = 0 singularity, from which everything in it must emerge, and able only to send matter and light out across the past horizon; the time reverse of the black-hole interior.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified by noting that past-directed curves fall from I' into II' just as future-directed ones fall from I into II.
prerequisites: Kruskal regions I, II, I', II'

concepts.name: time reversal of the primed universe
aliases: reversed Schwarzschild time in region I'
concepts.definition: In the second exterior I', the Schwarzschild time t increases toward the past as measured by the Kruskal T direction, so the primed side is a time-reversed copy of the unprimed side.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted in Section 27.2 when interpreting region II' as reached by past-directed world lines from I'.

concepts.name: non-traversability of the Schwarzschild wormhole
concepts.definition: No timelike or null curve connects exterior region I to exterior region I' in the Kruskal extension; any causal curve crossing a horizon ends on the future singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Answered first by inspection of 45-degree light cones on Fig. 27.1, then dynamically in Example 27.4 using a sequence of slices where the throat closes before a signal can cross.
prerequisites: Kruskal regions I, II, I', II'

concepts.name: dynamical evolution of the wormhole throat
concepts.definition: Following spacelike slices through both exteriors in order of increasing T, the geometry changes: early slices hit the past singularity and the two sheets are disconnected, then they touch at a pinch, open into a throat reaching radius 2M at T = 0, shrink, pinch again at the future singularity and separate.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 27.4 with the flip-book of embedding diagrams in Fig. 27.8; margin note 8 cautions that the choice of slicing is arbitrary.

concepts.name: static region of Schwarzschild
concepts.definition: Schwarzschild time translations t -> t + delta t leave the geometry unchanged and are timelike only in the exterior regions I and I'; inside the horizons the same shift is a spatial displacement, so there is no preferred static time and spatial slices through II or II' genuinely evolve.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening argument of Example 27.4, motivating why slices of the extension need not look the same at different T.
concepts.notes: In modern language: the Killing vector d/dt is timelike in I and I', null on the horizons and spacelike in II and II'. The book does not use Killing-vector language here.

concepts.name: embedding diagram
concepts.definition: A picture of a 2D slice (equatorial, fixed time) of a curved space drawn as a surface in flat 3D space so that distances within the surface are correct; used to show throats and funnels.
concepts.how_introduced: Used without re-derivation for the T = 0 wormhole slice (Fig. 27.7) and for the sequence of slices in Fig. 27.8.

concepts.name: Penrose diagram
concepts.definition: A compactified spacetime diagram obtained by a conformal rescaling that brings infinities to finite distance while keeping radial light rays at 45 degrees, so the whole causal structure fits on the page.
concepts.how_introduced: Section 27.3 reuses the Chapter 19 construction for the Kruskal extension, contrasting it with the Robertson-Walker diagrams.

concepts.name: conformal infinity
aliases: future and past null infinity scri+/-
concepts.definition: The boundary points and surfaces added in a Penrose diagram: future and past timelike infinity i+ and i- where timelike geodesics begin and end, spatial infinity i0, and future and past null infinity scri+ and scri- where light rays end and begin.
concepts.how_introduced: Named on Fig. 27.9 for both exteriors; their presence is attributed to asymptotic flatness, so each exterior corner looks like half of the Minkowski diagram.

concepts.name: spacelike singularity as boundary of spacetime
aliases: singularity at the edge of spacetime
concepts.definition: In a conformal diagram a curvature singularity is not an interior point but a boundary segment; for Schwarzschild both r = 0 singularities are spacelike horizontal edges at the top and bottom.
concepts.how_introduced: Emphasized in Section 27.3 and in the chapter summary, contrasting with Robertson-Walker spacetimes where every world line meets the singularity.

concepts.name: naked singularity
concepts.definition: A singularity from which causal signals can reach distant observers, i.e. one not hidden behind an event horizon, so that it could influence the future of the exterior.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in Section 27.3: the past (white-hole) singularity can send light into region I, which the authors call naked and attribute to the idealized extension rather than realistic collapse.
concepts.notes: Many authors reserve 'naked' for singularities forming in the future of regular initial data (e.g. in some collapse models) and simply call the Kruskal past singularity a white hole.

concepts.name: trapped surface
concepts.definition: A closed spacelike 2-surface (here a sphere of constant r) for which both the outgoing and the ingoing families of orthogonal future-directed light rays have decreasing area; in Schwarzschild every sphere with r < 2M is trapped.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 27.5 revisits the Chapter 26 motivation, using the constant-r grid of the Penrose diagram to show that inside the horizon both wavefronts move to smaller r.
prerequisites: Kruskal regions I, II, I', II'

concepts.name: relativistic Doppler shift
concepts.definition: An observer receding at speed v along a light wave's direction measures frequency Omega' = Omega sqrt((1 - v)/(1 + v)), obtainable by evaluating the wave phase Omega(T - X) along the observer's proper-time parametrized world line.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 27.5(a)-(b) as a warm-up for the accelerated observer.

concepts.name: exponential redshift of accelerated observer
concepts.definition: A uniformly accelerated observer receiving a light wave that chases it measures a frequency falling as Omega e^{-g tau}, because the wave phase along the hyperbola decays exponentially; this mirrors the exponential fading of signals from near a black-hole horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 27.5(c), explicitly framed as linking the redshift near horizons with the view of Schwarzschild coordinates as accelerating coordinates.
concepts.notes: This is the classical kernel of the Unruh and Hawking effects treated in Chapter 28.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild metric in null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Starting point carried over from Chapter 26: the radial part is a function of r times the flat light-cone form, but that function vanishes at r = 2M.
key_equations.symbols: U = t - r*, V = t + r*; r defined implicitly through r*

key_equations.name: Tortoise coordinate in terms of null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: The substitution that converts the troublesome factor 1 - 2M/r into an exponential of V - U.
key_equations.symbols: r* tortoise coordinate; U, V null coordinates

key_equations.name: Factorized two-dimensional metric
key_equations.meaning: The radial metric split into a factor regular at r = 2M, an exponential of the null coordinates, and the flat light-cone metric; the exponential is what the next substitution must remove.
key_equations.symbols: Follows from 1 - 2M/r = (2M/r)(r/2M - 1) and r/2M - 1 = e^{r*/2M} e^{-r/2M} outside the horizon

key_equations.name: Exponentiated (Kruskal) null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Change of null coordinates that absorbs the exponential factor; u < 0 and v > 0 in region I, and the ranges can be extended beyond.

key_equations.name: Product of the new null differentials (implicit step)
key_equations.meaning: The Jacobian of (27.3) exactly reproduces the exponential in (27.2), leaving 16M^2 times the regular factor.

key_equations.name: Metric in Kruskal null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Radial Schwarzschild metric as a regular conformal factor times -du dv; nothing special happens at r = 2M.
key_equations.symbols: Printed in the book as du du; it must be du dv.

key_equations.name: Kruskal time and space coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Converts null coordinates into a timelike and a spacelike one, so that -du dv = -dT^2 + dX^2.

key_equations.name: Kruskal metric
key_equations.meaning: The Schwarzschild geometry in a chart regular across the horizon: conformally flat in the T-X plane, with singular behaviour only at r = 0.

key_equations.name: Kruskal-Schwarzschild coordinate relations (also margin note 4)
key_equations.meaning: Implicit map between Schwarzschild (t, r) and Kruskal (T, X): r labels hyperbolae and t labels rays through the origin. The t relation as written holds in region I.
key_equations.symbols: Given in margin note 4 on p.281 and set as Exercise 27.2 on p.287

key_equations.name: Constant-t lines inside the horizon
key_equations.meaning: In the black-hole interior the roles of T and X in the t relation are exchanged, so constant-t lines are steep (timelike) rays.

key_equations.name: Horizon and singularity loci
key_equations.latex: r=2M:\ X^2-T^2=0\ \Rightarrow X=\pm T;\qquad r=0:\ X^2-T^2=-1
key_equations.meaning: Special members of the constant-r family: the horizon is a pair of null lines and the singularity a pair of spacelike hyperbolae.

key_equations.name: Hyperbolic (Rindler) coordinates, left and right wedges
key_equations.latex: T=x\sinh t,\quad X=x\cosh t,\quad Y=y,\quad Z=z
key_equations.meaning: Flat-space coordinates adapted to a family of uniformly accelerating observers; curves of constant x are hyperbolae X^2 - T^2 = x^2.
key_equations.symbols: (T, X, Y, Z) inertial; (t, x, y, z) accelerating

key_equations.name: Proper acceleration of a hyperbolic world line (Example 27.3 and margin note 6)
key_equations.meaning: Each constant-x curve is a world line of constant proper acceleration 1/x; smaller x means harder acceleration.

key_equations.name: Hyperbolic coordinates, top and bottom wedges
key_equations.latex: T=x\cosh t,\quad X=x\sinh t,\quad Y=y,\quad Z=z,\qquad X^2-T^2=-x^2
key_equations.meaning: Covers the future and past wedges, where T and X swap roles, just as t and r swap character inside a black hole.

key_equations.name: Rindler metric
key_equations.meaning: Minkowski space seen in accelerating coordinates; the metric degenerates at x = 0, the null boundary of the wedge, as Schwarzschild does at r = 2M.

key_equations.name: Metric in the top/bottom wedges
key_equations.meaning: In the future and past wedges x is timelike and t spacelike.

key_equations.name: Constant-t lines are straight (margin note 7)
key_equations.meaning: Rindler time is a hyperbolic angle, so its level sets are rays through the origin, like constant Schwarzschild t in Kruskal coordinates.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild-like form of the Rindler metric
key_equations.meaning: After x^2 = 2r - 1 (right/left wedges) or -x^2 = 2r - 1 (top/bottom), a single expression covers all wedges and mimics the structure -f dt^2 + f^{-1} dr^2 with f changing sign at r = 1/2.
key_equations.symbols: The book prints dx^2 in the second term; after the substitution it must be dr^2 (since dx^2 = dr^2/(2r - 1)).

key_equations.name: Analogy table
key_equations.meaning: Kruskal coordinates stand to Schwarzschild coordinates as inertial coordinates stand to a rocket's accelerating coordinates.

key_equations.name: Proper-time parametrization of uniform acceleration
key_equations.meaning: World line of an observer with constant proper acceleration g; reused as (27.16) in Exercise 27.5.
key_equations.symbols: g proper acceleration; tau proper time

key_equations.name: Inertial observer and plane wave (Exercise 27.5a)
key_equations.meaning: Set-up for reading off the observed frequency as the proper-time derivative of the wave phase along the world line.

key_equations.name: Relativistic Doppler shift
key_equations.meaning: Frequency seen by an observer receding along the wave's direction at speed v.

key_equations.name: Exponential redshift for uniform acceleration
key_equations.meaning: Along the hyperbola T - X = -e^{-g tau}/g, so the observed frequency decays exponentially in proper time: the flat-space counterpart of the fading of signals from near a horizon.

figures.label: Fig. 27.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: The full Kruskal plane: thick curves mark the r = 0 singularities; a collapsing star lives only in regions I and II, while I' and II' are explained in the wormhole section.
figures.visual_description: Square X-T diagram with arrowed axes. Two bold diagonals through the origin (r = 2M) split it into four boxed regions: I on the right, II at the top, I' on the left, II' at the bottom. Thin hyperbolae of constant r fill all four regions (opening sideways in I and I', up/down in II and II'), and thin straight lines of constant t fan out from the origin in every quadrant. Bold hyperbolae at top and bottom mark r = 0, with the area beyond them shaded dark grey. Rotated labels at the top right identify the curve families: r = 0, r < 2M, r = 2M, r > 2M.
figures.what_it_teaches: The complete coordinate grid of the Kruskal extension at a glance: horizons as null diagonals, the four regions, and singularities as spacelike boundaries.
concepts: Kruskal regions I, II, I', II'

redesign.idea: Layered Kruskal explorer: a canvas of the X-T plane where the learner toggles grids (constant r, constant t), region shading and light cones, and hovers any point to see its Schwarzschild (t, r) values or 'undefined' labels.
redesign.interaction: Hover to read (t, r) and the region name; checkboxes for grid families; a slider for M rescales labels; clicking a point draws its future light cone clipped by the singularity.

figures.label: Fig. 27.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Kruskal plane with selected constant-r curves, satisfying T^2 - X^2 = (1 - r/2M) e^{r/2M}.
figures.visual_description: X-T axes with the two diagonals (r = 2M) and grey-shaded regions beyond the bold r = 0 hyperbolae. In region I, two thin hyperbolae open to the right, labelled r = 2.4M (closer to the horizon) and r = 2.8M. In region II, two thin hyperbolae lie between the horizon and the singularity; their tiny stacked label is hard to read but their positions match about r = 1.8M (nearer the horizon) and r = 1.4M. Labels are placed at the upper right.
figures.what_it_teaches: How a fixed radius becomes a hyperbola: timelike outside the horizon, spacelike inside, and why r must decrease once one is in region II.

redesign.idea: Radius slider: drag r from 3M down to 0 and watch the corresponding hyperbola sweep in from the right, collapse onto the diagonals at 2M, flip orientation and rise to the singularity.
redesign.interaction: Slider for r/M; the hyperbola updates and is coloured by causal character (timelike/null/spacelike); an inset shows the function (1 - r/2M) e^{r/2M} with the current value marked.

figures.label: Fig. 27.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Kruskal plane with straight constant-t lines: T/X = tanh(t/4M) outside and X/T = tanh(t/4M) inside.
figures.visual_description: X-T axes, diagonals and shaded singularity regions as before. In region I, five rays from the origin are labelled t = 2.5M, t = M, t = 0 (along the X axis), t = -M and t = -2.5M, fanning between the horizons. In region II, five steep rays from the origin run up into the shaded area, labelled from left to right t = -2.5M, -M, 0 (the T axis), M, 2.5M. The diagonals carry labels t = infinity (upper right and lower left) and t = -infinity (upper left and lower right).
figures.what_it_teaches: Schwarzschild time is a hyperbolic angle; the horizon lines are t = +/-infinity, so no finite Schwarzschild time labels a horizon crossing.

redesign.idea: Boost-angle dial: a rotating ray whose angle is set by t/4M, shown simultaneously in region I and II, with a counter that runs off to infinity as the ray approaches the diagonal.
redesign.interaction: Drag a handle to change t; the ray in each region updates; a readout shows tanh(t/4M) and flags the change from spacelike to timelike ray when moving from region I to II.

figures.label: Fig. 27.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: An infalling timelike world line drawn on the Kruskal diagram.
figures.visual_description: Kruskal axes with diagonals and shaded singularity regions. A single world line enters from the lower right in region I below the X axis, climbs up and slightly to the left with arrowheads, crosses the X axis and then the diagonal X = T, and ends on the future r = 0 hyperbola a little to the right of the T axis. Three small hourglass-shaped light cones with 45-degree sides sit on it (below the X axis, on the X axis, and just past the horizon), showing that its slope always stays steeper than the light rays.
figures.what_it_teaches: The horizon crossing is unremarkable locally; once past X = T, every future-directed path, including the infaller's, ends on the singularity.

redesign.idea: Steer-the-probe game: the learner pilots a spacecraft on the Kruskal diagram with a velocity slider constrained to lie inside the local light cone and tries to escape after crossing X = T.
redesign.interaction: Arrow keys or drag set the direction within the cone; the path is traced and proper time accumulated; when inside region II every allowed direction is shown to intersect the singularity.

figures.label: Fig. 27.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Light pulses sent by a fast infalling astronaut and received by an observer holding a fixed radius.
figures.visual_description: Kruskal axes, with the future diagonal labelled r = 2M and shaded singularity regions. In region I a thin hyperbola (the hovering observer) has its vertex just right of the X axis and its upper branch bends up toward the future horizon. The astronaut is a straight line that starts far down at the lower right, runs up-left almost parallel to the X = -T diagonal (only slightly steeper than 45 degrees, i.e. falling very fast), crosses the X axis and the future horizon, and ends on the future singularity where it meets the T axis. A dense ladder of parallel 45-degree segments leaves the astronaut's line heading up and to the right: rungs emitted outside the horizon end on the observer's hyperbola, spaced ever wider along it, while rungs emitted after the crossing run parallel to the horizon and end on the singularity near the upper right corner.
figures.what_it_teaches: Received pulse intervals grow without bound as emission approaches the horizon, and no pulse from inside reaches the outside: the Chapter 25 results as pure geometry.

redesign.idea: Pulse ladder with a live clock comparison: the astronaut emits pulses at equal proper-time spacing, and a plot beside the diagram shows arrival times on the hovering observer's clock diverging.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for the astronaut's infall speed, the observer's radius and pulse spacing; press play to animate emission; hover a rung to see emission and reception proper times and the ratio.

figures.label: Fig. 27.6(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Accelerated particles in flat space as hyperbolae in the right wedge; horizontal bars at fixed T show that the rear of a rigid body must accelerate harder than the front.
figures.visual_description: Minkowski T-X axes with the two 45-degree lines through the origin. In the right wedge three hyperbolae are labelled x = 1 (closest to the null lines), x = 2 and x = 3. Three short horizontal bars at increasing T join the hyperbolae, forming a small ladder above the X axis; the bars shorten and shift right as T grows.
figures.what_it_teaches: Uniformly accelerated observers are hyperbolae; a rigid rocket corresponds to a set of nested hyperbolae with different accelerations, and is length-contracted in the inertial frame.

redesign.idea: Rigid rocket builder: stack observers along a rocket at chosen positions and watch their hyperbolae and required accelerations, with the rocket's inertial-frame length shrinking while each crew member's radar-measured length stays fixed.
redesign.interaction: Drag the rocket's front and back x values; play time to animate; readouts give each end's proper acceleration 1/x and the lab-frame length at the current T.

figures.label: Fig. 27.6(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The accelerating coordinates drawn in all wedges, with hyperbolae in region I (constant x) and region II; the picture looks like a Kruskal diagram.
figures.visual_description: Minkowski T-X axes with bold 45-degree lines dividing the plane into boxed regions I (right), II (top), I' (left), II' (bottom). Region I holds three sideways-opening hyperbolae labelled x = 1 (closest to the null lines), x = 2 and x = 3. Region II holds three upward-opening hyperbolae whose rotated labels at the upper right read t = 1 (nearest the null lines), t = 2 and t = 3. No curves are drawn in I' or II'. Note that eqn 27.8 makes the region II curves constant x, so the printed t labels (and the caption's 'constant t') do not match the text.
figures.what_it_teaches: Visual identity between the Rindler-wedge picture of flat space and the Kruskal diagram, supporting the analogy table (27.12).
concepts: Kruskal regions I, II, I', II'

redesign.idea: Morphing twin diagrams: flat space in hyperbolic coordinates on the left, Kruskal on the right, with a slider interpolating the labels and conformal factor so learners see what is literally the same and what differs (singularity hyperbolae appear only on the right).
redesign.interaction: Slider from 'Rindler' to 'Kruskal'; matched hover highlighting between panels; toggle to show where the book's region II labels differ from eqn 27.8 (constant x).

figures.label: Fig. 27.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: The T = 0 slice of Kruskal spacetime drawn as a throat between universe I (upper sheet) and universe I' (lower sheet). The caption calls it a timelike slice, but it is spacelike.
figures.visual_description: Hand-drawn perspective sketch: two flat rectangular sheets, one above the other, each covered with a wavy coordinate mesh, joined by a vertical tube that flares into each sheet. Dotted circles mark where the tube meets each sheet. The upper sheet is labelled R^3.
figures.what_it_teaches: The spatial geometry of the maximal extension is a wormhole joining two asymptotically flat regions, with a narrowest sphere of radius 2M.

redesign.idea: 3D Flamm-paraboloid wormhole with a draggable ring measuring circumference/2 pi, showing the radius bottoming out at 2M at the throat and growing into both sheets.
redesign.interaction: Orbit camera; drag a ring along the surface to read areal radius r and proper radial distance from the throat; toggle to show the corresponding T = 0 line on a mini Kruskal diagram.

figures.label: Fig. 27.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: How slices of Kruskal spacetime change as T increases (caption again says timelike, but they are spacelike).
figures.visual_description: Left: a Kruskal diagram with crossed diagonals, arrowed T axis, X and -X marked, and hatched hyperbolae for the past and future singularities. Three horizontal lines are labelled A'-A (low, cutting the past singularity), B'-B (T = 0) and C'-C (high, cutting the future singularity). Right: a column of paired embedding surfaces. For A/A' and C/C' each pair is two separate sheets with a pointed dimple (cusp) aimed at the other; for B/B' the sheets are connected by a wide throat.
figures.what_it_teaches: The wormhole is dynamical: disconnected sheets, pinch, throat of maximum radius 2M at T = 0, pinch, disconnected again. This is why nothing can cross.
concepts: dynamical evolution of the wormhole throat

redesign.idea: Wormhole flip-book: scrub a horizontal slice through the Kruskal diagram and watch the 3D embedding morph from two cusps to a throat and back, while a light pulse launched from region I is animated along both views and hits the singularity before reaching the far sheet.
redesign.interaction: Slider for slice height T (with an option for tilted slices, illustrating footnote 8's arbitrariness); play button launches a radial light pulse; 3D view rotates.

figures.label: Fig. 27.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: Panel (a): conformal (Penrose) picture of the fully extended Kruskal spacetime with its regions and infinities labelled. Panel (b): the same outline overlaid with curves of fixed Schwarzschild r and fixed t.
figures.visual_description: (a) A horizontally stretched hexagon with T and X axes. Flat top and bottom edges (double lines) are labelled r = 0. Diagonals marked r = 2m cross at the centre, making regions II (top), I (right), I' (left), II' (bottom). Corners at the ends of the top and bottom edges are i+ and i-; the left and right tips are i0; the slanted outer edges are scri+ (upper) and scri- (lower) on both sides. (b) The same outline densely filled with curved grid lines converging on the corners. Arrows label families 'r = constant' and 't = constant'; hatched top and bottom edges are labelled 'Future singularity r = 0' and 'Past singularity r = 0'. In I and I', constant-r curves bow between i- and i+ and constant-t curves fan from the centre to i0; in II and II' the pattern is rotated.
figures.what_it_teaches: Global causal structure in a finite picture: two exteriors each with Minkowski-like infinities, spacelike singular edges, and how the grid rotates across horizons (the basis of the trapped-surface argument).
concepts: spacelike singularity as boundary of spacetime
Kruskal regions I, II, I', II'

redesign.idea: Kruskal-to-Penrose compactifier: a slider continuously applies the arctan compactification to the Kruskal grid so learners watch hyperbolae become the bowed curves and infinity pull in to the corners, with light rays staying at 45 degrees throughout.
redesign.interaction: Compactification slider from 0 (Kruskal) to 1 (Penrose); toggle grid families; click to emit a flash and see its ingoing and outgoing fronts, colour-coded by whether r grows or shrinks.

worked_examples.label: Example 27.1
worked_examples.problem: Starting from the radial Schwarzschild metric in null coordinates, rewrite the factor 1 - 2M/r using r* = (V - U)/2, then remove the remaining exponential with a further coordinate change.
worked_examples.method: Exponentiate the tortoise relation to get r/2M - 1 = e^{-r/2M} e^{(V-U)/4M}, substitute into 1 - 2M/r, then define u = -e^{-U/4M}, v = e^{V/4M} so du dv contains the same exponential; the text continues with T and X on the next page.
worked_examples.key_insight: The metric factors into a regular function of r, an exponential in the null coordinates, and a flat light-cone metric; the coordinate singularity lives entirely in the exponential, which a change of null coordinates can absorb, exactly as for Rindler space.
worked_examples.result: ds^2 = -(2M/r) e^{-r/2M} e^{(V-U)/4M} dU dV, then ds^2 = -(32M^3 e^{-r/2M}/r) du dv.

worked_examples.problem: Complete the construction of the Kruskal metric and relate old and new coordinates.
worked_examples.method: Set T = (u + v)/2, X = (v - u)/2 so that -du dv = -dT^2 + dX^2, restore the angular part, and from uv = -e^{r*/2M} and -v/u = e^{t/2M} obtain T^2 - X^2 = (1 - r/2M) e^{r/2M} and T/X = tanh(t/4M).
worked_examples.key_insight: Finite, non-zero conformal factor at r = 2M proves the horizon singularity is a coordinate effect; conformal flatness in T-X puts every radial light ray at 45 degrees.
worked_examples.result: Kruskal metric (27.6) with relations in margin note 4 / (27.13).

worked_examples.problem: Map Schwarzschild structures onto the Kruskal plane: where are r = 2M, r = 0, constant r, constant t, and which region does the original chart cover?
worked_examples.method: Read the implicit relations: fixed r fixes X^2 - T^2 (hyperbolae), r = 2M gives X = +/-T, r = 0 gives T^2 - X^2 = 1; fixed t fixes a ratio T/X or X/T (rays); check signs to place r > 2M in X > |T| and r < 2M in T > |X|.
worked_examples.key_insight: Schwarzschild (t, r) is a hyperbolic-polar chart on half of the plane (T > -X); t is an angle running from -infinity to infinity within each quadrant.
worked_examples.result: Four regions; Schwarzschild coordinates cover I and II only.
concepts: Kruskal regions I, II, I', II'

worked_examples.label: Example 27.2
worked_examples.problem: Describe an astronaut falling into the hole on a Kruskal diagram, and the light pulses the astronaut sends to an observer staying at fixed radius.
worked_examples.method: Draw the astronaut's world line always steeper than 45 degrees from region I across X = T into region II; draw the hovering observer as a constant-r hyperbola; join emission events to the hyperbola with 45-degree lines.
worked_examples.key_insight: Because the observer's hyperbola asymptotes to the horizon, successive 45-degree rays hit it at ever later times, and any ray leaving the astronaut inside region II can never reach X > T.
worked_examples.result: Pulses arrive increasingly rarely, with arrival time diverging for emission near the horizon; pulses from inside end at the singularity together with the astronaut.

worked_examples.label: Example 27.3
worked_examples.problem: Explain why Kruskal coordinates are natural by comparing with uniformly accelerated coordinates in flat spacetime.
worked_examples.method: Write T = x sinh t, X = x cosh t (and the sinh/cosh swap for the top and bottom wedges), compute the transformed metric -x^2 dt^2 + dx^2 (or its sign-swapped version), substitute x^2 = +/-(2r - 1) to obtain a single Schwarzschild-like form, and tabulate the correspondence.
worked_examples.key_insight: Schwarzschild coordinates behave like the coordinates of a rocket crew: they cover only a wedge, have a degenerate time component at the wedge boundary, and use a hyperbolic angle as time. Kruskal coordinates play the inertial role.

worked_examples.label: Example 27.4
worked_examples.problem: Given that the wormhole slice at T = 0 appears to connect two universes, follow how spacelike slices of the extension change with T and decide whether anything can pass through.
worked_examples.method: Argue that time translation is a symmetry only in regions I and I', so slices through II and II' need not be identical; take horizontal slices at several T and draw each as an embedding diagram.
worked_examples.key_insight: The connection between universes is transient: it forms from a pinch at the past singularity, opens to radius 2M at T = 0 and pinches off at the future singularity faster than any causal signal can cross.
worked_examples.result: No traveller or signal gets from I to I'; it ends at r = 0.
concepts: dynamical evolution of the wormhole throat

worked_examples.label: Example 27.5
worked_examples.problem: Use the Penrose diagram with constant-r and constant-t lines to compare how a spherical light flash spreads outside and inside the horizon.
worked_examples.method: Emit at a point P in region I and step up to the next future 'side-to-side' grid line, noting whether outgoing and ingoing fronts are at larger or smaller r; repeat at a point Q in region II, where side-to-side lines are constant r.
worked_examples.key_insight: Inside the horizon the future direction is the direction of decreasing r, so both fronts shrink: the spheres are trapped, which is the mechanism signalling the singularity from Chapter 26.
worked_examples.result: Region I: outgoing front grows, ingoing shrinks. Region II: both shrink; closed trapped surfaces.
concepts: Kruskal regions I, II, I', II'

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Inertial versus rocket coordinates in flat space: Minkowski coordinates are to Rindler coordinates as Kruskal coordinates are to Schwarzschild coordinates.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Rebuilds the reader's intuition about which chart is natural: the Rindler wedge has a degenerate metric on its null boundary, a hyperbolic-angle time and a mirror wedge, exactly like the Schwarzschild exterior, so the awkwardness of Schwarzschild coordinates is attributed to their 'accelerated' character.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Minkowski space is flat everywhere and has no singularity; the Schwarzschild interior ends at r = 0 and is curved. The book's global substitution x^2 = 2r - 1 only mimics the shape of the metric; the accurate statement is that Schwarzschild near its horizon is approximately Rindler.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side flat-space rocket and black-hole diagrams with synchronized cursors; a zoom slider on the black-hole side magnifies the neighbourhood of the horizon until the grid becomes indistinguishable from the Rindler one.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A hovering observer outside a black hole is like a passenger in a constantly thrusting rocket.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Both world lines are hyperbolae on the respective inertial-like diagram; the observer in Example 27.2 is explicitly kept in place by a rocket.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The hovering observer's required acceleration grows without bound near r = 2M and depends on r in a way the Rindler model reproduces only close to the horizon.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Thrust meter: drag the hovering radius toward 2M and watch the required proper acceleration climb while the hyperbola hugs the horizon.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A rigid rocket: its tail must push harder than its nose.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Horizontal bars between hyperbolae at equal T in Fig. 27.6(a) and margin note 6 show nested hyperbolae with accelerations 1/x.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only a side remark here; not connected explicitly to the gravitational redshift between the top and bottom of a hovering tower, which it naturally explains.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A white hole is a black hole run backward in time.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Region II' is defined by symmetry with II: past-directed curves fall into it from I' as future-directed ones fall from I into II, so everything in II' comes out of the past singularity.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Time-reversal symmetry of the vacuum solution does not imply white holes form in nature; realistic collapse removes regions I' and II'.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Play/reverse toggle on the Kruskal diagram that reflects T -> -T, turning an infall animation into an emission from the white hole.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The throat as a tube joining two sheets of paper.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Fig. 27.7's embedding picture gives a concrete spatial image of the two universes joined at radius 2M.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: It shows a single slice and tempts the reader to think one could walk through; Example 27.4 is needed to show the tube exists only fleetingly and cannot be crossed.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A bridge that collapses before a runner can cross it.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Example 27.4 narrates the throat opening and pinching shut too fast for any signal to reach the far side.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The 'speed' of pinching depends on the slicing, which is arbitrary (margin note 8); the invariant statement is the causal one read from light cones.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Race animation: a light pulse travels along the embedding surface as the throat closes; learners adjust the launch time and always lose.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The singularity as the edge of the map rather than a place on it.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: spacelike singularity as boundary of spacetime
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The Penrose diagram places both r = 0 singularities on the boundary, alongside the infinities, reinforcing the Chapter 19 view.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Boundary language is intuitive but the precise notion of a singular boundary is subtle and not developed.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Synge's remark: had spherical symmetry been approached with good coordinates, no one would have suspected a singularity at the horizon.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Encouragement in margin note 5 to push through the unfamiliar coordinates by stressing that they are the simplest description.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Schwarzschild radius is a real singularity where spacetime breaks down.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In Kruskal coordinates all metric components are finite and regular at r = 2M; only r = 0 is singular.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Schwarzschild metric components diverge there and infinite coordinate times appear in calculations.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Kruskal coordinates are an artificial mathematical trick with no physical naturalness.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They are the analogue of inertial coordinates; Schwarzschild coordinates are the awkward, accelerated-frame description.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The definition is implicit and exponential and seems pulled from nowhere.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Each point of the Kruskal diagram is a single event.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The angular coordinates are suppressed, so each point represents a whole 2-sphere of area 4 pi r^2.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Two-dimensional spacetime diagrams usually show events.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The wormhole in the Kruskal extension lets a traveller reach another universe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: No timelike or null curve connects I and I'; the throat pinches off before any signal can cross, and every crossing path ends at r = 0.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The T = 0 embedding picture looks like an open tunnel.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Schwarzschild geometry is static everywhere, so its spatial slices never change.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Time-translation symmetry is timelike only in regions I and I'; inside the horizons t is spacelike and slices genuinely evolve.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The metric components do not depend on t, suggesting a static solution throughout.
concepts: dynamical evolution of the wormhole throat

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A black hole formed by a collapsing star comes with a second universe and a white hole.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only regions I and II are relevant to a collapsing star; the star's interior replaces the rest, and the visible past singularity is attributed to the idealized extension.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The vacuum Kruskal diagram is shown as 'the' black-hole spacetime.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The future singularity r = 0 is a point at the centre of the black hole that one could avoid by steering sideways.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In the Kruskal and Penrose diagrams r = 0 is a spacelike line lying in the future of every event in region II; it is a moment, not a place, so no steering avoids it.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Everyday language of a 'central point', and r = 0 being the origin in flat space.
concepts: spacelike singularity as boundary of spacetime

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Light emitted anywhere just outside the horizon never reaches a distant observer.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Every pulse emitted outside r = 2M eventually arrives, though the arrival time grows without bound as the emission point approaches the horizon; only light emitted on or inside the horizon never arrives.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book's phrasing that pulses just above the horizon arrive at t -> infinity can be read as 'never'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The hyperbolae in the top wedge of the Rindler picture are world lines of accelerating observers.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Curves X^2 - T^2 = -x^2 are spacelike; no observer can follow them. They are the analogues of constant-r surfaces inside a black hole.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The text refers to 'accelerating world lines in regions I and II', and the curves look like rotated copies of the region I hyperbolae.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Schwarzschild time t measures the passage of time everywhere, so t = infinity on the horizon means the infaller never crosses.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: t is a hyperbolic angle that labels the whole horizon line with a single value t = infinity; the infaller crosses at finite proper time and finite Kruskal T.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Coordinate time is what distant observers use, and it diverges along the infall.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Because a black hole is a region where r < 2M, a hovering observer could stay at fixed r inside it with enough thrust.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Constant-r curves inside the horizon are spacelike hyperbolae; following one would require moving faster than light.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Outside, fixed r is achievable with thrust, and the diagram tour lists constant-r curves in all regions alike.

thought_experiments.name: The astronaut's farewell pulses
thought_experiments.setup: An astronaut falls radially into a Schwarzschild black hole, sending regular light pulses to a colleague who hovers at fixed radius with rockets.
thought_experiments.lesson: Received intervals stretch without limit as the astronaut approaches the horizon; pulses emitted inside never arrive; all of this is visible from 45-degree rays on the Kruskal diagram.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Animated pulse ladder with receiver clock plot (see Fig. 27.5 redesign).

thought_experiments.name: Coordinates inside an accelerating rocket
thought_experiments.setup: A rocket accelerates uniformly through empty space; its crew labels events with coordinates adapted to their motion (hyperbolic Rindler coordinates).
thought_experiments.lesson: The crew's chart covers only a wedge, has a horizon and a degenerate metric on it, just as Schwarzschild coordinates do; inertial coordinates remove the problem, as Kruskal coordinates do.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Rocket crew view versus inertial view of the same set of events, with a toggle to show the Rindler horizon.

thought_experiments.name: Trying to cross the wormhole
thought_experiments.setup: A traveller in universe I heads for the throat hoping to emerge in universe I'.
thought_experiments.lesson: The light-cone structure forbids it; seen as a sequence of slices, the throat closes before the traveller reaches its middle, and the traveller meets r = 0.
concepts: dynamical evolution of the wormhole throat

thought_experiments.name: A flash inside and outside the horizon
thought_experiments.setup: A spherical light flash is set off at an event outside the horizon and another inside, and the areas of the outgoing and ingoing fronts are tracked.
thought_experiments.lesson: Outside, the outgoing front grows; inside, both fronts shrink because the future points toward smaller r: trapped surfaces.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Click-to-flash on the Penrose diagram with area readouts of both fronts.

thought_experiments.name: Chasing a light wave with constant acceleration
thought_experiments.setup: An observer with constant proper acceleration g moves along a hyperbola while a plane light wave comes up from behind.
thought_experiments.lesson: The measured frequency decays as e^{-g tau}: acceleration alone yields the exponential redshift characteristic of horizons.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Wave crests drawn at 45 degrees on a Minkowski diagram crossing a hyperbolic world line, with a live frequency readout on a log scale.

historical_notes.year: 1960 (publication of the coordinates; year not given in the book)
historical_notes.event: Kruskal, known mainly for work on solitons, introduced the global coordinates for the Schwarzschild geometry that bear his name.
historical_notes.significance: Gave the first widely used maximal chart of the Schwarzschild solution, settling the nature of r = 2M.

historical_notes.year: 1960 (Szekeres's relativity paper; not given in the book)
historical_notes.event: Szekeres independently found equivalent coordinates; a margin note adds that his work with Esther Klein on a combinatorial geometry problem led to their marriage, prompting Erdos to call it the Happy Ending problem.
historical_notes.significance: Explains the double name of the coordinates and adds a human aside.

historical_notes.event: The authors quote Synge's observation that a better initial choice of coordinates would have prevented anyone from thinking the horizon singular.
historical_notes.significance: Synge had himself studied the global structure of Schwarzschild before Kruskal (1950, not stated in the book); the quote frames the chapter's message.

historical_notes.event: The analogy between accelerating coordinates in flat space and Schwarzschild coordinates is credited to Rindler.
historical_notes.significance: Supplies the conceptual bridge used throughout the chapter and in Chapter 28's Unruh discussion.

applications_and_observations.topic: Infall of an astronaut and signals to a hovering observer
applications_and_observations.details: Example 27.2's qualitative picture. Own estimate: for a solar-mass hole the horizon has r_S = 2GM/c^2 of about 2.95 km, and the maximum proper time from horizon to singularity for a radial fall is pi GM/c^3, roughly 15 microseconds.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimates: r_S(1 solar mass) about 2.95 km; pi GM/c^3 about 1.5e-5 s.

applications_and_observations.topic: Exponential fading of signals near the horizon
applications_and_observations.details: The Kruskal exponent 1/4M sets the e-folding time of redshift seen far away (derived in Chapter 26, echoed in Exercise 27.5). Own estimate: 4GM/c^3 is about 20 microseconds for one solar mass and about 85 s for Sagittarius A* (4.3 million solar masses).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimates: 4GM/c^3 about 2.0e-5 s (1 solar mass), about 85 s (4.3e6 solar masses).

applications_and_observations.details: The T = 0 slice has minimal areal radius 2M. Own estimate: for a ten-solar-mass hole this is about 30 km, but the throat is not traversable and does not exist for collapsed stars.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: r_throat = 2GM/c^2; own estimate about 30 km for 10 solar masses.

applications_and_observations.topic: Collapsing stars use only regions I and II
applications_and_observations.details: Fig. 27.1's caption and the naked-singularity remark indicate that astrophysical black holes formed by collapse do not possess the second exterior or the white hole; the eternal Kruskal extension is an idealization.

applications_and_observations.topic: Proper acceleration of uniformly accelerated observers and Rindler horizons
applications_and_observations.details: An observer at Rindler coordinate x has proper acceleration 1/x (Exercise 27.4 asks for a direct covariant computation). Own estimate in SI units: an acceleration of 9.8 m/s^2 puts the Rindler horizon c^2/g behind the observer, about one light-year.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimate: c^2/g about 9.2e15 m (about 0.97 light-year) for g = 9.8 m/s^2.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Geometric units G = c = 1; mass M has dimensions of length and the Schwarzschild radius is r_S = 2M.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Fig. 27.9 labels the horizon as r = 2m (lowercase).

notation_and_conventions.convention: (-, +, +, +): timelike intervals have ds^2 < 0; the Kruskal metric has -dT^2 + dX^2.
dOmega^2 = dtheta^2 + sin^2 theta dphi^2; dropped from intermediate steps and restored at the end.
Capital U = t - r*, V = t + r* are Eddington-Finkelstein null coordinates; lowercase u = -e^{-U/4M}, v = e^{V/4M} are the exponentiated Kruskal null coordinates.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Reversed from Chapter 26's Rindler example, where lowercase u, v were logarithmic and capital U, V exponentiated.

notation_and_conventions.convention: T = (u + v)/2 timelike, X = (v - u)/2 spacelike, both dimensionless; r = 0 at T^2 - X^2 = 1.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Other texts sometimes rescale by 4M or use different letters (e.g. U, V or u, v for Kruskal null coordinates).

notation_and_conventions.convention: I (our exterior), II (black-hole interior), I' (second exterior), II' (white-hole interior).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Other books often use I, II, III, IV in varying order.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Kruskal and Penrose diagrams suppress the 2-sphere; radial light rays at 45 degrees; future is up; singularities drawn as thick, jagged, hatched or double lines with the region beyond shaded.
(t, x, y, z) denote accelerating coordinates and (T, X, Y, Z) inertial ones; x is the inverse proper acceleration.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The letters t and x clash with Schwarzschild t and the Kruskal X; the tutor should disambiguate.

notation_and_conventions.convention: i+ future timelike, i- past timelike, i0 spatial infinity; scri+ and scri- future and past null infinity.
g denotes proper acceleration, tau proper time, Omega the wave's angular frequency in the inertial frame; acceleration vector a = nabla_u u.

margin_notes.summary: Epigraph from Thomas Hardy's Two on a Tower reflecting that stars are not eternal but burn out.
Biography of Martin Kruskal (1925-2006), a mathematical physicist best known for solitons.
Biography of George Szekeres (1911-2005) and the story of the Happy Ending problem with Esther Klein, named by Erdos.
The angular term r^2 dOmega^2 is untouched by the manipulations, so it is omitted during the example and put back at the end.
Gives the inverse relations between Kruskal and Schwarzschild coordinates: T^2 - X^2 = (1 - r/2M) e^{r/2M} and t/4M = artanh(T/X).
Encourages readers who find the coordinates heavy going, reminding them that the payoff is simplicity, and quotes J. L. Synge on the horizon singularity being an artefact of the coordinates.

Each constant-x curve is a particle with acceleration 1/x; for a rigid rocket the rear must accelerate more than the front, so its inertial-frame length contracts progressively (horizontal bars of Fig. 27.6a).
Because X/T = coth t, constant-t lines in the hyperbolic coordinates are straight lines through the origin.
Caution that no spacelike slicing is singled out; the evolution in Fig. 27.8 uses an arbitrary choice.
