difficulty.notes: The algebra is short and largely a repeat of the Rindler calculation, but the conceptual load is high: implicit coordinates, t as a hyperbolic angle, regions not covered by the original chart, time-reversed universes, dynamical wormholes and conformal compactification all arrive within nine pages. Diagrams carry most of the argument, which helps visual learners but means OCR-quality figure labels matter. Several printed slips (du du in 27.4, dx^2 in 27.11, 'timelike slice' captions, region II labels in Fig. 27.6b, 'I' and I'') can confuse a careful reader.

teaching_gems.gem: Present the Schwarzschild calculation as a replay of the Rindler calculation: same three moves (null coordinates, exponentiate, sum and difference), different function.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners who survived the flat-space toy model recognise each step, so the new difficulty is only bookkeeping and the method becomes a transferable recipe.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Two-column step-through derivation: Rindler on the left, Schwarzschild on the right, advancing together with matching steps highlighted.

teaching_gems.gem: Factorize the metric into a regular piece, an exponential of null coordinates, and the flat light-cone form before choosing the new coordinates.
teaching_gems.why_effective: It shows precisely what the coordinate change must accomplish, turning an apparently magical substitution into an obvious one.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Colour-coded equation where the learner drags candidate substitutions onto the exponential factor and sees which choice cancels it.

teaching_gems.gem: Flip the intuition: Kruskal coordinates are the inertial ones and Schwarzschild the accelerated ones (analogy table 27.12).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Replaces 'weird coordinates' with a familiar special-relativity picture and explains why Schwarzschild t freezes at the horizon.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Synchronized rocket-in-flat-space and hovering-near-black-hole diagrams with a horizon-zoom slider.

teaching_gems.gem: Once every radial light ray is at 45 degrees, answer causal questions by eye: can a path from I reach I'? can a pulse from II escape?
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners check claims themselves with a ruler instead of trusting integrals, which builds durable causal intuition.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Causal-connectivity puzzle: pick two events; the app shades the future light cone of the first and asks whether the second is reachable before revealing the answer.

teaching_gems.gem: Tell the wormhole story as a flip-book of slices so non-traversability is seen as the throat closing too fast.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Converts an abstract causal theorem into a vivid dynamic image, while margin note 8 keeps the slicing honest.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Scrubbable T slider linking a Kruskal slice line to a morphing 3D embedding with a racing light pulse.

teaching_gems.gem: Read trapped surfaces off a grid on the Penrose diagram by stepping to the next future side-to-side line and asking whether r went up or down.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A simple, repeatable visual test that makes 'the future points to smaller r inside' concrete.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Click-a-flash tool on the gridded Penrose diagram displaying the areas of the outgoing and ingoing spheres one step later.

teaching_gems.gem: Hovering observer as a hyperbola receiving a ladder of 45-degree pulses.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The crowding of rungs near the horizon makes infinite delay and redshift visually self-evident.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Animated pulse ladder with live plot of reception interval versus emission proper time.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive exponential redshift from a plane wave's phase along an accelerated hyperbola (Exercise 27.5).
teaching_gems.why_effective: A two-line calculation connects horizons, acceleration and redshift, setting up Unruh/Hawking physics without quantum theory.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Minkowski diagram with 45-degree wave crests crossing a hyperbolic world line; slider for g; log-scale plot of measured frequency against proper time.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed eqn 27.4 reads 'du du' instead of 'du dv'.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A careful reader may think the metric is degenerate or that u alone appears.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the corrected form -(32M^3 e^{-r/2M}/r) du dv and include the Jacobian step du dv = e^{(V-U)/4M} dU dV/16M^2.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqn 27.11 keeps dx^2 after substituting x^2 = 2r - 1; the correct term is (2r - 1)^{-1} dr^2. The resemblance to Schwarzschild is also only schematic (a linear function 2r - 1 vs 1 - 2M/r).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may try to verify the substitution and fail, or conclude that flat space literally is Schwarzschild.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the corrected metric and supplement with the precise near-horizon statement: with rho = sqrt(8M(r - 2M)), the Schwarzschild t-r metric is approximately -rho^2 (dt/4M)^2 + drho^2, i.e. Rindler with time t/4M.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 27.6(b) labels the region II hyperbolae 't = 1, 2, 3' and its caption says region II shows constant t, while eqn 27.8 makes those curves constant x; the text also calls them accelerating world lines, though they are spacelike.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confuses which coordinate is timelike inside the wedge and suggests observers can move along spacelike curves.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Label them constant x (timelike coordinate in that wedge) and describe them as analogues of constant-r surfaces inside the horizon, not as world lines.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Captions of Figs 27.7 and 27.8 call the slices 'timelike', but they are spacelike hypersurfaces (the text says so).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Undermines the distinction between spatial slices and world lines just when the wormhole argument depends on it.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Refer to them consistently as spacelike slices at fixed T.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Typo: the primed universe is described as 'regions I' and I''' where I' and II' is meant.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Minor, but region labels are the backbone of the discussion.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Sign handling across regions is glossed: u = -e^{-U/4M}, v = e^{V/4M} and t/4M = artanh(T/X) are valid in region I; inside the horizon the absolute value in r* flips a sign (u > 0), and regions I', II' require further sign choices.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners attempting to verify region II or I' relations get sign contradictions.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Tabulate the signs of u and v in each quadrant (I: u<0<v; II: u,v>0; I': v<0<u; II': u,v<0) and derive the relations separately in each.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Null-coordinate letters swap roles between Chapter 26 (lowercase logarithmic, capital exponentiated) and Chapter 27 (capital logarithmic, lowercase exponentiated); Example 27.3 also reuses t and x for Rindler coordinates.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Easy to substitute the wrong definition when combining results from the two chapters.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: In the app, use distinct symbols (e.g. U_EF, V_EF for Eddington-Finkelstein; U_K, V_K for Kruskal; eta, rho for Rindler).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The throat is described as formed by 'the two singular r = 0 lines', but the narrowest sphere of the T = 0 slice is the r = 2M bifurcation sphere at the origin of the diagram.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think the wormhole throat is at the singularity.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Point to the origin X = T = 0 as the throat (a 2-sphere of radius 2M) and explain that the singularities cut off slices at larger |T|.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Calling the past singularity 'naked' is non-standard; most texts reserve the term for singularities not hidden by horizons that arise in the future of regular data, and simply call this a white hole.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may carry an imprecise definition into later reading on cosmic censorship.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Define naked singularity carefully and note that the white-hole singularity is visible but belongs to an idealized eternal solution.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 27.2 says pulses emitted just above the horizon reach the observer only as t -> infinity, which blurs 'arbitrarily late' and 'never'.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Reinforces the misconception that nothing outside the horizon can be seen.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Stress that each pulse from r > 2M arrives at finite t; only the limit of emission at the horizon has infinite delay.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: No explicit mention that realistic collapse replaces regions I' and II' by the stellar interior; only the Fig. 27.1 caption hints at it.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may believe observed black holes contain wormholes and white holes.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Juxtapose the Kruskal Penrose diagram with the collapse diagram of Chapter 25 (Fig. 25.11) and shade the part of the extension that survives.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The statement that the metric is static only in regions I and I' is made without Killing-vector language or a demonstration of why t becomes spacelike inside.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Leaves 'increments in t are increments in space' as an assertion.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show g_tt = -(1 - 2M/r) changes sign at r = 2M and draw the vector d/dt as a boost-like field on the Kruskal diagram (timelike in I and I', spacelike in II and II').

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 27.5's preamble says the exponential horizon redshift was seen 'in this chapter', but it was derived in Chapter 26.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may search this chapter in vain.

tutor_notes: Opening question: 'Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates let things fall in smoothly. What goes wrong for light trying to come out, and why would we want one chart that handles both?' Then recall the Rindler toy model before touching Schwarzschild.

Order of explanation: (1) Rindler recap and its three-step recipe; (2) factorized Schwarzschild metric; (3) exponentiate and form T, X; (4) the regular conformal factor; (5) diagram tour; (6) infall and pulses; (7) Rindler analogy; (8) extension, wormhole and white hole; (9) non-traversability; (10) Penrose diagram and trapped surfaces.

Check for understanding: ask the learner to place on a blank Kruskal diagram the horizon, r = 0, a hovering observer, and the line t = 0 inside and outside. Common error: drawing r = 0 as a point or constant t inside as horizontal.
Check: 'Why must T/X = tanh(t/4M) hit the diagonal only as t -> infinity?' A correct answer mentions that tanh never reaches 1, so Schwarzschild time cannot label the horizon.

When a learner asks 'is the other universe real?', separate the mathematics (the vacuum solution naturally extends) from physics (collapse removes I' and II'; the extension is an idealization), and mention that astrophysical black holes are expected to follow the collapse diagram of Chapter 25.
When asked 'can I go through the wormhole?', first let them try with 45-degree lines on the diagram; then show the slice flip-book. Emphasize the causal argument is slicing-independent.
Correct the book's slips explicitly when they appear: du dv in 27.4, dr^2 in 27.11, spacelike (not timelike) slices, region II curves in Fig. 27.6(b) are constant x and not world lines.

For advanced learners, give the sharper form of the analogy: near r = 2M, with proper distance rho = sqrt(8M(r - 2M)), the metric becomes -rho^2 d(t/4M)^2 + drho^2. So 1/4M is the surface gravity and the Kruskal exponent is not arbitrary.
For beginners, stay with pictures: light at 45 degrees, hyperbolae of constant r, rays of constant t. Skip the implicit inverse relations until they can read the diagram.

Common learner question: 'Why is T called time if the infaller's clock is proper time?' Answer: T is a coordinate chosen to make light cones simple; no observer's clock equals T in general, just as Minkowski t is only one observer's time.

Common learner question: 'If t is spacelike inside, what is time inside the black hole?' Answer: r decreases toward the future; the constant-r hyperbolae in region II are successive moments ending at r = 0.
Bridge to Chapter 28: after Exercise 27.5, ask what a thermometer on the accelerating rocket might read, and why the same logic could make a black hole glow.
